name: Umar Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I buy rice, cooking oil, spices, canned goods and halal meat for Tidewater Foodservice in Bellmouth. We supply about a hundred and eighty restaurants, school canteens and care homes. I start by checking the overnight orders, then I'm on the phone with suppliers and importers, and I use an AI tool once or twice a week to draft emails and check contract wording. I like the feeling of keeping people fed. What tires me is the pay, which is lower than my cousins in other trades, and the way prices change by the hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's probably right, and thank God for common sense. At work I'd say let's keep using the tools for what they're good at and not get carried away. At the mosque I'd say, nothing changes, so keep doing good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be glad but not relaxed. We have a mortgage, Ibrahim is twelve and Maryam is eight, and we have under a month of savings. My wife Zainab is a teaching assistant, which is steady but not well paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep using the tools for emails, and work on saving even a little. I'd keep the family's giving, because that matters to us, but I'd trim the rest. And I'd talk to my manager about a raise, because I haven't asked in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grateful, mostly, but with a knot under it. A peaceful week is rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In a world where AI changes little, what still weighs on your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the school term starts, the uniforms and books arrive in the same month as the mortgage bill. We pay with the card and then spend the next two months catching up. If one of our wages stumbled, we'd feel it in the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Tidewater to treat buyers fairly: a yearly review, honest talk about pay and some say in how targets are set. I'm not asking for charity. I'm asking to be paid for the risk I carry when a supplier fails.

say: I'd say **common sense** wins: use the tools for what they're good at.
At the mosque I'd say keep doing **good work**.
think: I'd be glad but **not relaxed**; under a month of savings and a mortgage.
do: Keep using AI for **emails** and trim the extras.
Keep our **giving**, but cut the rest.
Ask my manager for a **raise** after three years.
S0.quote: The uniforms and books arrive in the same month as the mortgage bill. We pay with the card and then spend the next two months catching up.
fieldNote: Faith and community give him **steadiness**, but money gives him the knot.
Asks for **fair pay** for risk, not charity, consistent with free-market views.
Plans to **protect giving** while trimming other spending.

steps.text: Ask my manager for a raise at the yearly review
Save thirty a week before the school year starts
Trim takeaways and streaming but keep our monthly giving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of business, and people should adapt. I'd say at the mosque that we should help the ones who lose work, and train our young people for trades and skills that last. I wouldn't ask the government to rescue everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm concerned. Much of what I do is on that card: reordering, comparing prices, booking deliveries, answering customers. I use the tools a bit, but I'm not an expert. I'd be one of the buyers they keep or one they don't, and I can't tell which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more and learn from the younger staff. I'd learn the software, then ask to be the one who manages it. I'd also build my relationships with the restaurant owners, because they trust a person. And I'd start saving more, and put an end to anything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I believe in work, so I don't like the thought of my work being taken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reordering and price comparison go first. Dealing with restaurant owners who want a special price, or a late delivery before Eid, needs a person. That's the part I'd protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tidewater look in three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably four buyers become two, and the others are given other roles. I'd want to be useful in the second group. And there's Reggie, who does our deliveries planning, who might be the first to go.

say: I'd say change is part of **business** and people should adapt.
At the mosque I'd say help those who **lose work** and train young people in lasting skills.
think: Much of my work is **on that card**: reordering, comparing prices, booking deliveries.
I can't tell whether I'd be **kept** or not.
do: Learn from the **younger staff** and ask to manage the software.
Build ties with **restaurant owners**, who trust a person.
feel: **Uneasy**; I believe in work, so losing it feels wrong.
S1.quote: Dealing with restaurant owners who want a special price, or a late delivery before Eid, needs a person.
fieldNote: He relies on **relationships** with restaurant owners.
Free-market belief: adapt through **work**, not rescue.
Honest that he cannot tell if he would be **kept**, which feeds his unease.

steps.text: Ask the younger buyers to teach me the reorder software
Visit twenty restaurant owners to deepen the relationships
Save forty a week and cut the extras

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a serious test for everyone and we need to hold together. I'd say we should look after families first, as a community. And I'd say governments and companies should answer plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be alarmed. If AI can do any thinking work, my job goes quickly, and there are few buying jobs nearby. We have almost nothing saved. I'd have to act at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk with Zainab and our families about what we can lean on. I'd cut spending to the basics. I'd ask the mosque and my brothers about work in their trades. And I'd try to start a small supply service for home caterers and small restaurants, where I already know the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest tightens when I think of the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would let me train and build slowly. Two years doesn't. I'd have to take what's there and also start something. I'd lean on family, because that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly desk and phone. What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years for robots gives my brothers' trades more breath. I'm a desk man, and I'd be asked to become something else. A small business might be the thing that bridges those three years.

say: I'd say this is a **serious test** and we should hold together.
I'd say families come first, with **community** help.
think: If AI does any thinking work, my job goes **quickly**, and few buyer jobs exist here.
do: Lean on **family** and cut spending to the basics.
Ask the mosque and my **brothers** about work in their trades.
Start a **supply service** for small caterers I know.
feel: **Alarmed**; my chest tightens when I think of the children.
S2.quote: I'm a desk man, and I'd be asked to become something else.
fieldNote: Turns to **family and the mosque** first.
Sees a **small supply business** as a bridge.
Admits being a **desk man** whose work goes first, and does not pretend otherwise.

steps.text: Ask my brothers and the mosque about work in their trades
Cut spending to the basics and pause extra giving
Supply spices and rice to small home caterers I know
Apply for delivery coordination jobs at larger depots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance, and we should prepare. I'd say we should teach the young people trades and real skills. I'd say it's better to build than to complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious, but with hope. Five years gives me time to build a small business and save a cushion. I believe if you work hard and plan, you can find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start the supply business in the evenings with two or three restaurants I know well. I'd save for six months of bills. I'd take a short sales and account management course, which is a skill that lasts. And I'd learn the AI tools properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with hope and a plan. Hope is important to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What do you do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ibrahim and Maryam to learn how to work with people, to be honest and to learn a skill that serves others. I'd tell them that the work is changing, but good character isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Ibrahim and Maryam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd try to build my own list of customers, because that's the thing no one can take from me. I know the owners and the cooks. A customer list is like a field you've planted.

say: I'd say five years is a **chance**, and it's better to build than complain.
I'd say we should teach young people **real skills**.
think: I'd be anxious, but with **hope**; five years lets me build a small business.
If you work hard and plan, you can **find a way**.
do: Start the **supply business** in the evenings with two or three restaurants.
Take a **sales** and account management course.
S3.quote: A customer list is like a field you've planted.
fieldNote: Hope and **faith in effort** keep him from feeling alarmed.
Wants his children to value **character**, which he says does not change with technology.

steps.text: Start supplying two restaurants in the evenings by spring
Save six months of bills in a separate account
Complete a short sales and account management course
Use AI weekly to draft quotes and contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if we use it well. I'd say our schools should return to teaching skills, and that employers should invest in their people. At the mosque I'd say, plan with trust, and don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly settled. By 2036 I'm fifty-three, and I'd have time to build something. I'd still carry the worry that my savings are thin, and the mortgage is long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Tidewater, save steadily, and learn the tools better each year. I'd build my side supply business slowly, perhaps hiring one person eventually. I'd also try to grow my own skills in sales, which is a safer skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A little restless, because I can't see the whole road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this still feel important?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Tidewater for training on company time, and a promise to move buyers into new roles before they're let go. From the community, I'd ask for what we already do: neighbours helping neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of your employer, or your community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still feels important, because 2036 is not so far. But I won't let it spoil today. I'd live carefully and still enjoy the children's years.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** if we use it well.
At the mosque I'd say **plan with trust**, don't panic.
think: I'd feel **fairly settled**; by 2036 I'd have time to build something.
My **savings** are thin and the mortgage is long.
do: Carry on at Tidewater and **save steadily**.
Build a **side supply business** slowly, perhaps hiring one person.
Grow my **sales** skills, a safer skill.
S4.quote: I won't let it spoil today. I'd live carefully and still enjoy the children's years.
fieldNote: Time lets him **plan with trust**, as faith teaches.
Still counts **thin savings** and a long mortgage as the real weight.
Asks for **paid training** and early moves into new roles.

steps.text: Save an extra fifty a month toward six months of bills
Grow the supply side business to ten customers by 2031
Learn the reorder tools better each year at work
Take a part-time sales qualification over three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, with no doubt. There's no time to build, and no savings to fall back on. What would help is employers who give honest notice, training that is paid for and leads to real work, and a community that stands together. I'd also like a simple way to start a small business without drowning in forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps that I'm not afraid of hard work or change. I'm afraid of being caught unprepared, with children who depend on me. I believe a person can always do something with an honest effort, but I'd like to be given the time.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of hard work or change. I'm afraid of being caught unprepared, with children who depend on me.
portrait: **Umar Evans**, 43, buys rice, oil and halal meat for Tidewater Foodservice in Bellmouth, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
His **wife Zainab** is a teaching assistant; they have two children, Ibrahim and Maryam, and a mortgage.
He uses AI **now and then**, relies on relationships with restaurant owners and trusts faith and community.
His mood runs from **uneasy** to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, and his answer is a small supply business.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there's no time to build and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice** from employers, paid training into real work, and **simple** small-business paperwork.
